author: blueiridium.
content:
Hello, there is another slashing-related issue that I have been testing, I didn't know if I should add it here or the consensus dev channel. 

This one seems like it might be a design choice, and I’m not sure whether it’s a known tradeoff your teams have intentionally made. It’s a possible proposer-lookahead grinding path in EIP-8045, proposed for Glamsterdam.

If an operator controls the final proposer slot of epoch k, it can include valid evidence slashing another validator it owns. EIP-8045 excludes that key before calculating the k+2 proposer lookahead. The operator knows the RANDAO reveal it would put in its block, so it can compare publishing normally, withholding the block, and publishing with different one-key self-slashes before deciding what to do. This reallocates existing proposer duties; it does not create slots or increase stake.

In a private 128-validator Lighthouse/Geth network, a signed self-slash block became canonical and both CL peers agreed on 10 owned k+2 duties versus 9 under either control: +1 net duty. Separately, a mainnet-sized synthetic selector replay with 921,428 validators and about 25% owned effective stake found a best +7 duties over both controls (6 to 13) when screening every other owned key at naturally owned final slots. An ownership-layout sensitivity run found +9 (7 to 16) in one 25% map and +5 in one 5% map. In some layouts, choosing to slash mattered, but the choice of which key added no further control.

The +7, +9, and +5 results are selector-only counterfactuals. We have not reproduced those gains with signed blocks on a full-size client network or measured how often they occur on mainnet.

author: potuz
content: Just for the record as I'm not going to be in the call. I think this problem should not be fixed. Also I think the numbers are less than what reported since a staker that owns 25% of the stake can also influence lookahead by revealing or not in the last few slots for free. The cost should be compared with that existing attack that a 25% attacker already can perform quite often since they'll get the last 4-5 bits in an epoch quite regularly

author: jtraglia

author: blueiridium.
content: One thing I want to clarify: the final-slot proposer may have a choice over which of its own validators to slash, and that choice can affect the k+2 lookahead even if only one validator is slashed. I wasn’t sure that came through in my original post. I believe the proposed fix addresses this too, but the additional context might still be useful. An operator with more validators could have more candidate schedules to compare, although many choices produce the same outcome depending on how its validators are distributed across the registry. That distribution was difficult to model realistically for a real operator. I hope my read of the situation, the EIP, and the outcomes makes sense and is accurate. Thanks!
